cues.x: The Intelligent Investor, by Benjamin Graham.
There is a nineteen year old boy standing at the back of a bookshop in Omaha, Nebraska, in the spring of nineteen fifty.
He has already read every book about investing in the Omaha public library, some of them twice.
He is bright, he is arrogant in the way that clever nineteen year olds are, and he has been chasing charts and hot tips and patterns for years, with mixed results.
He picks up a book published the year before by a man he has never met, and he reads it, and he later says it changed his life.
He says it was like seeing the light.
He calls it, decades later, by far the best book on investing ever written, and he says the copy he bought is one of his most valuable possessions.
That boy was Warren Buffett.
The book was this one.
And what makes the story worth telling is not that a great investor liked a book.
It is what he says the book gave him.
Buffett is clear about it: what he got was not stock tips, or a screening formula, or a way to predict the market.
What he got was a sound intellectual framework for making decisions, and a way to keep his emotions from corroding it.
That is his phrase.
To invest successfully over a lifetime, he wrote in the preface to the edition most of us now read, does not require a stratospheric IQ, unusual business insights, or inside information.
It requires that framework, and emotional discipline.
He then says something rather brutal about his own teacher's book: the parts you need are chapters eight and twenty, and if you cannot make yourself read the rest, at least read those two.
We will get to chapters eight and twenty, and they are the heart of what I want to give you today.
But first you need to know who wrote this, because Graham did not derive these ideas in a seminar room.
He paid for them.
Benjamin Graham was born in London in eighteen ninety four and brought to New York as a baby.
His father ran an import business and died when Benjamin was nine, and the family fell hard and fast out of comfort into genuine poverty.
His mother, trying to recover their position, opened a margin account and speculated in stocks, and then came the panic of nineteen oh seven, and she was wiped out.
Graham grew up watching his mother's dignity stripped away by the market.

He was a brilliant student, won a scholarship to Columbia, and on graduation was offered teaching positions in three separate departments, English, mathematics and philosophy, which tells you something about the size of the mind involved.
He turned them all down because the family needed money, and went to Wall Street as a runner delivering securities, at twelve dollars a week.
He was extraordinarily good at it, and by his thirties he was running his own fund.
And one story from that period tells you everything about how his brain worked.

In the mid nineteen twenties, Graham was studying obscure filings that companies made to the Interstate Commerce Commission, documents almost nobody read, and he found something peculiar in the filings of the Northern Pipe Line Company.
This was a small, dull pipeline business.
Its shares traded at around sixty five dollars, and it paid a six dollar dividend, so on the surface it looked like an ordinary sleepy holding.
But buried in those regulatory filings was the fact that Northern Pipe Line was sitting on a portfolio of high grade railroad bonds worth about ninety five dollars a share.
Ninety five dollars of liquid securities, having nothing to do with running a pipeline, inside a company whose stock you could buy for sixty five.
Graham went to management and suggested, reasonably, that the bonds be sold and the cash distributed to the owners of the business, who were the shareholders.
Management showed him the door.

So he bought stock, a great deal of it, went to the annual meeting, was procedurally out-maneuvered, came back the following year having gathered proxies, won himself a seat on the board, and forced the distribution.
Shareholders received seventy dollars a share in cash and still owned the pipeline.
He had bought a dollar for sixty five cents by doing the reading nobody else would do.
And then, in nineteen twenty nine, the market fell apart, and Graham, who was smart and careful and who understood value better than nearly anyone alive, got destroyed.
His fund lost roughly seventy percent from nineteen twenty nine through nineteen thirty two.
He spent years earning it back.
It took him until nineteen thirty five to make his investors whole.
He was in his late thirties, and he had just learned, at enormous cost, that being right about value is not enough if you have not built in room to be wrong about timing.
That experience is the reason this book exists in the shape it does.
Every insistent, repetitive, almost nagging piece of caution in it was bought with real money and real years.
So let us take the ideas.
The first thing Graham does, on the very first pages, is draw a line that most people in finance blur on purpose.
He separates investment from speculation.
His definition is precise, and I want to read it to you almost exactly, because the wording matters.
An investment operation, he says, is one which, upon thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return.
Operations not meeting these requirements are speculative.
Notice what is packed in there.
Thorough analysis, meaning you have actually studied the business.
Safety of principal, meaning protection against serious loss under all normal or reasonably likely conditions.
And an adequate return, note the word adequate, not spectacular, not market beating, adequate.
Anything that does not meet all three is speculation.
Not a sin, Graham says, but it must be called by its name.

His warning, delivered over and over across five hundred pages, is that most people who believe they are investing are actually speculating, and the reason they do not notice is that speculation dressed in the vocabulary of investing feels responsible.
He is scathing about a particular category: the person who buys a stock because it has been going up, and calls that analysis.
If there is one sentence to tattoo somewhere, it may be his rule that you should never buy something merely because it has risen, or sell merely because it has fallen.

Graham does allow that a person who cannot resist speculating should do it in a strictly separated account, with a small amount of money they can genuinely afford to lose, and never, ever add more to that account after a loss.
He is a realist about human nature.
He just wants the two activities kept in different rooms.
The second structural idea is that there are two kinds of intelligent investor, and you have to decide honestly which one you are.
He calls them the defensive investor and the enterprising investor.
And this is where nearly everyone misreads him.
Those labels are not about risk appetite.
They are not conservative versus aggressive.
They are about effort.
The defensive, or passive, investor is someone who wants freedom from bother and effort, and whose principal aim is to avoid serious mistakes.
The enterprising, or active, investor is someone willing to devote real time and care to the selection of securities, and who expects a better than average return as payment for that work.
Graham is emphatic on the point that the enterprising investor is not taking more risk.
He is doing more work.
The extra return, if it comes, is wages for labor, not compensation for danger.
And he is equally emphatic that the middle position, the person who does a little work, dabbles, follows some tips, reads a bit, is the worst place to stand.
That person takes on the disadvantages of activity without doing enough of it to earn anything.
As he puts it, most of the time you would do better to be thoroughly passive than half active.
For the defensive investor, Graham gives a policy so simple it almost sounds like a joke, and yet it has held up remarkably well for seventy five years.
Split your money between high grade bonds and a diversified list of leading common stocks.
Never hold less than twenty five percent in stocks, and never more than seventy five percent.
The remainder goes in bonds.
The simplest version is fifty fifty.
And then, crucially, rebalance.
When stocks have run up and grown to sixty percent of the portfolio, you sell some to get back to your target.
When they have collapsed to forty percent, you buy.
Sit with what that mechanism actually does.
It forces you to sell into strength and buy into weakness, automatically, without requiring you to have any opinion about the future at all.
It converts the emotional problem into an arithmetic one.
Graham's view was that the defensive investor's greatest enemy is the temptation to act on how things feel, and the simplest defense is a rule that acts for you.
He also recommends dollar cost averaging, putting the same amount in at regular intervals regardless of price, for the same reason.
Not because it is optimal in some mathematical sense, but because it is a policy a nervous human being can actually follow through a bad decade.
Before the two famous chapters, Graham does something that I think is quietly one of the most useful exercises in the book.

He walks the reader through a century of stock market history, roughly eighteen seventy one to nineteen seventy one, decade by decade, not to find a pattern to trade on but to inoculate you against the belief that the recent past is the permanent future.
The lesson he draws is uncomfortable for anyone who has just lived through a good stretch.
Every generation, he observes, discovers a reason why the old rules of valuation no longer apply, and every generation discovers, usually about three years later, that they do.
He points at the late nineteen twenties, when a genuinely new and prosperous economy convinced people that stocks were permanently safe at any price.
He points at the aftermath, when the same people concluded that stocks were permanently unsafe at any price, which was equally wrong and cost them the entire recovery.
His argument is not that history repeats in detail.
It is that the emotional cycle repeats exactly, and that the confident language used to justify each extreme is remarkably similar each time.
There is an almost eerie example of this sitting inside the book's own publishing history.
When Graham prepared the nineteen seventy three revision, the fashionable belief on Wall Street was in a group of large, high quality growth companies that everyone called the Nifty Fifty.
Xerox, Polaroid, Avon, Eastman Kodak and the rest.
The received wisdom was that these were one-decision stocks: so excellent, so certain to keep growing, that the only decision was to buy, and price was essentially irrelevant.

Graham, unfashionably, kept insisting that price is never irrelevant, that a wonderful company bought at a foolish multiple is a poor investment, and that the arithmetic does not care how much you admire the business.

The book came out, and the market promptly fell by roughly half over nineteen seventy three and seventy four, and several of those untouchable companies lost seventy, eighty, ninety percent of their value and took decades to recover.
Some never did.
That is the practical purpose of his history chapter.
Not prediction.
Vaccination.
Now let us go to chapter eight, one of the two Buffett says you must read.
It contains the single most useful metaphor in the history of investing, and Graham introduces it almost casually.
Imagine, he says, that you own a small share in a private business that cost you a thousand dollars.
One of your partners is a man named Mr. Market.
He is a very obliging fellow.

Every single day, without fail, he turns up and tells you what he thinks your interest is worth, and he offers either to buy you out at that price or to sell you an additional stake on the same terms.
Sometimes his valuation seems plausible and justified by what you know about the business.
But quite often, Mr. Market lets his enthusiasm or his fears run away with him, and the value he proposes seems to you a little short of silly.
Some days he is euphoric, and can see nothing but favorable factors ahead, and he names an enormous price, because he is terrified you will snap up his interest and rob him of imminent gains.
Other days he is despondent, can see nothing but trouble ahead, and names a very low price, desperate to unload his stake before things get worse.
Now, Graham says, here is your position, and it is an enviable one.
Mr. Market's daily communication does not obligate you to do anything at all.
You may ignore him entirely, and he will not be offended.
He will be back tomorrow with a new quotation.
If you like, you may take advantage of him: sell to him when he is manic, buy from him when he is depressed.
But the truly disastrous thing, the thing that ruins people, is to let Mr. Market's mood become your own.
To decide that because he is offering a low price, the business must be in trouble, and to sell out of fear.
To decide that because he is offering a high price, the business must be wonderful, and to buy out of greed.
The market, in other words, is there to serve you, not to instruct you.
Its prices are quotations, not verdicts.
And that reframing, which sounds almost trivially simple, is the thing Buffett built a career on.
He has said that if you understand chapters eight and twenty and you have the emotional discipline, you cannot get a bad result in investing.
Which leads directly to what may be the most quoted line in the book.
Graham writes that the investor's chief problem, and even his worst enemy, is likely to be himself.
Not the economy.
Not the Federal Reserve.
Not the analysts or the fund managers or the algorithms.
You.

The person who panics at the bottom and gets excited at the top, and who will do so again, and who therefore needs rules and structures built in advance, while calm, to protect them from the version of themselves that shows up during a crash.
He follows that with a sentence about market forecasting that I would put on the wall of every brokerage.
He says that the investor with a portfolio of sound stocks should expect their prices to fluctuate, and should neither be concerned by sizable declines nor excited by sizable advances.
He should always remember that market quotations are there for his convenience, either to be taken advantage of or to be ignored.
He should never buy a stock because it has gone up or sell one because it has gone down.

And he adds, with characteristic dryness, that he would not be far wrong if this motto were shortened to, never buy a stock immediately after a substantial rise or sell one immediately after a substantial drop.
Now chapter twenty, the other essential one.

It is titled Margin of Safety as the Central Concept of Investment, and Graham opens it by saying that if he were challenged to distill the secret of sound investment into three words, he would venture the motto: margin of safety.
What does it mean?
It means that you do not buy something at what you calculate it is worth.
You buy it substantially below what you calculate it is worth, and the gap between the two is your protection.
His analogy is from engineering.
When you build a bridge, you calculate the load it must carry, and then you build it to hold a great deal more than that.
You build it to carry thirty thousand pounds and you drive ten thousand pound trucks across it.
You do not do that because you expect a thirty thousand pound truck.

You do it because your calculations might be wrong, the steel might have a flaw, the load might be badly distributed on a windy day, and because the cost of being slightly wrong about a bridge is catastrophic.
The margin of safety serves exactly that function in a portfolio.
It is not there because you expect to be wrong.
It is there because you might be, and because your estimate of a company's value rests on judgments about the future that are, at best, approximations.
If you buy a business at a price that assumes everything goes well, then anything less than everything going well produces a loss.
If you buy it at a price that assumes things go moderately badly, you can be wrong about several things and still come out fine.
Graham then makes the point that turns this from a technique into a philosophy.
The function of the margin of safety, he says, is to render unnecessary an accurate estimate of the future.
You will never know the future.
Nobody does.
So build a position that does not require you to.
And in the same chapter comes the sentence Buffett has called the nine most important words ever written about investing: investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike.
Graham means that literally.
When you buy a share, you are not buying a ticker or a squiggle on a chart.
You are buying a fractional ownership in an actual enterprise that has revenues, debts, factories, employees and customers.
Behave the way you would if you were buying the corner shop outright.
Nobody buys a laundromat because the price of laundromats has been rising.
They look at the accounts.
From that principle he draws four business rules, and they are worth hearing in full because they are so plain.
One: know what you are doing.
Know your business.
Do not try to make manufacturing profits out of securities, meaning do not expect a return well above what a business owner would earn without doing the analysis a business owner would do.
Two: do not let anyone else run your business unless you can both supervise their performance with adequate care and understanding, and have unusually strong reasons for trusting their integrity.
That rule, written decades before the modern fund industry, is the whole of due diligence in one sentence.
Three: do not enter upon an operation, meaning do not buy something for a profit, unless a reliable calculation shows it has a fair chance of yielding a reasonable profit.
Stay away from ventures where you have little to gain and much to lose.
And four: have the courage of your knowledge and experience.
If you have formed a conclusion from the facts, and you know your reasoning is sound, act on it, even though others may hesitate or differ.
He adds the line that follows from all of it: you are neither right nor wrong because the crowd disagrees with you.
You are right because your data and reasoning are right.
Now, what does the actual work look like?
Graham does give concrete criteria, and while the specific numbers are dated in places, the logic behind each one still teaches.
For the defensive investor picking individual stocks, he lists seven requirements.
Adequate size, because tiny companies are more vulnerable to a single bad year.
A sufficiently strong financial condition, which he defines with the current ratio, current assets at least twice current liabilities, and long term debt not exceeding net current assets.
Earnings stability, meaning positive earnings in each of the past ten years, no exceptions.
An uninterrupted dividend record going back twenty years.
Earnings growth of at least a third in per-share earnings over ten years, using three-year averages at each end to smooth out flukes.
A moderate price to earnings ratio, not more than fifteen times average earnings of the past three years.
And a moderate ratio of price to assets, not more than one and a half times book value.

He then offers a rule of thumb combining the last two, which people now call the Graham number: the price to earnings ratio multiplied by the price to book ratio should not exceed twenty two and a half.
So you can pay a higher multiple of earnings if you are paying less relative to assets, and vice versa.
You will notice these screens are almost cruelly strict.
That is the point.
Graham was not trying to find the best companies.
He was trying to build a filter that made it very hard to buy something dangerous.
For the enterprising investor, he goes further, into the technique that made his own reputation and that is still called net-net investing.
Take a company's current assets, the cash, the receivables, the inventory.
Subtract every single liability the company has, all of it, short term and long term, as though the business were being liquidated tomorrow.
What is left is the net current asset value.
Graham's proposal was to look for companies whose entire market capitalization was less than two thirds of that number.
Think about what that means.

You would be buying the company for less than the value of its liquid assets after paying off all the debt, and getting the factories, the brands, the equipment and whatever future the business has entirely for free.
Graham's firm ran this strategy across roughly thirty years and it returned about twenty percent a year.

He was careful to say it only works applied to a diversified group, thirty positions or more, because individually many of these companies are ugly for good reason and some of them will keep deteriorating.
Bought as a basket, the arithmetic wins.
There is a wonderful irony buried in Graham's own career that he was gracious enough to write about himself, and it complicates the picture in a way I think you should hear.

In nineteen forty eight, his firm, Graham-Newman, bought half of a small automobile insurance company called Government Employees Insurance Company, GEICO, for about seven hundred and twelve thousand dollars.
That purchase broke Graham's own rules.

It was far too large a fraction of the fund to put in one place, it was not a cheap statistical bargain of the net-net variety, and regulators eventually made the firm distribute the shares to its own investors because a fund was not supposed to own that much of an insurer.
And over the following twenty odd years, that single holding grew to be worth more than the whole of everything else Graham-Newman had done put together.
All the careful, diversified, painstaking bargain hunting across decades, and one concentrated bet on a fine business bought at a fair price outweighed it.

Graham noted the moral himself, with characteristic honesty: that there is more than one road to investment success, that a single brilliant decision coupled with a lucky break may outweigh a lifetime of methodical journeyman work, and that behind the brilliant decision there usually stands preparation and a disciplined mind.
It is also, quietly, the seed of what his most famous student would go on to do.

Buffett began as a strict Graham cigar-butt buyer, hunting statistically cheap and often mediocre businesses, and, pushed by Charlie Munger, evolved toward buying excellent businesses at reasonable prices.
The margin of safety idea survived that evolution completely intact.
Only the source of the safety changed, from the balance sheet to the durability of the business itself.
Graham also has a chapter on the investor and his advisers, which is short and rather bracing.

His position is that most people receive their investment advice from parties who are paid for transactions rather than for outcomes, and that this is not a scandal, it is simply a structure you should understand before you act on the advice.

He asks you to notice who is compensated by what, to be deeply suspicious of anyone promising unusual results, and to hold to a plain principle: the more enthusiasm a stranger has for making you rich, the more slowly you should move.

He argues that the defensive investor who wants help should look for advisers whose function is conservation rather than performance, and should treat the promise of beating the market as, in itself, a warning sign.
Graham devotes a great deal of the book to warnings, and they are unfashionably useful.
On new issues, that is, initial public offerings, he is merciless.
His observation is structural rather than cynical.
A company chooses when to sell shares to the public.
It will choose the moment most favorable to the seller, which is by definition the moment least favorable to the buyer.
New issues arrive in floods during bull markets and vanish during bear markets, which tells you all you need to know about what drives the timing.

He advises the defensive investor to simply skip them entirely, and notes that many will show attractive price gains early and then, when the enthusiasm passes, fall to a fraction of the offering price.
On earnings figures, he devotes an entire chapter to the ways in which reported profits can be dressed up, and it reads as though it were written last year.

He warns about special charges taken to make future years look better, about pension accounting, about depreciation choices, about the difference between a company's reported earnings and what its owners actually got.
His instruction is to look at earnings averaged over seven to ten years, because that smooths out both the manipulation and the cycle, and to treat any single year's number as nearly meaningless.
On growth stocks, he is careful rather than dismissive.
He acknowledges that a genuinely fast growing company can justify a high price.

His objection is that the market's estimate of future growth is usually optimistic, that yesterday's fastest growers frequently disappoint, and that the price paid to participate is usually so high that even good growth produces a poor return.

He offers a rough formula to illustrate the arithmetic, valuing a company at its current normal earnings multiplied by eight and a half plus twice the expected annual growth rate, and then immediately warns readers not to take it too seriously, because the moment you have a formula you start believing your own growth estimate.
He also spends time on inflation, a subject that was becoming urgent when he revised the book in the early nineteen seventies.
His conclusion was more sober than the received wisdom.

Stocks are often described as an inflation hedge, and over long periods they have offered real protection, but he showed that the relationship is far from reliable and that there have been long stretches where it failed entirely.
His answer was, again, diversification and a policy rather than a prediction.
Underneath all the specific rules sits an idea Buffett later nicknamed Aesop's investment formula, from the old line about a bird in the hand being worth two in the bush.
Every investment, whether a bond, a share, a farm or a flat, is fundamentally the same transaction: you hand over a certain sum of money today in exchange for an uncertain stream of money later.
So there are only ever three questions.
How much cash will actually come out of it.
When will it come.
And how sure are you.
Everything else, the charts, the momentum, the headlines, the opinions on television, is noise dressed as analysis.
Graham's whole apparatus exists to answer those three questions conservatively, and his margin of safety exists because the answer to the third one is always, less sure than I think.
This is also why Graham is so insistent on realistic expectations.

He wants you to notice that a stock's long term return comes from real, boring, countable sources: the dividend you receive, the growth in the company's earnings, and any change in the multiple people are willing to pay for those earnings.
The first two are business results.
The third is a popularity contest.
Over a year or two, the popularity contest dominates completely and the business results are invisible.
Over twenty years, it is almost entirely the other way around.
Which means the investor who cannot wait is playing a game of sentiment, while the investor who can wait is playing a game of arithmetic.
Graham thought only one of those two games could be reliably won.
Zweig, in his commentary, adds a modern layer to this that Graham would have enjoyed.
He points out that the research on how our brains handle money is not flattering.
Financial gains and losses activate the same circuitry as more primal rewards and threats.

A repeated pattern, even a random one, triggers anticipation after only two or three occurrences, which is why a stock that has risen three days running feels like it has a momentum that in fact does not exist.
Losses register with roughly twice the emotional force of equivalent gains, which is why perfectly sensible people liquidate sound holdings at the bottom.
Zweig's conclusion is a restatement of Graham's own: the biggest risk you face is not sitting in the market.
It is sitting between your ears, and the only reliable defense is a written policy made in advance, when nothing is at stake, and then honored when everything is.
Now, there are two more things you should know to hold this book honestly.

The first is that the version most people read, the one you would buy today, is the nineteen seventy three revision with extensive commentary by the financial journalist Jason Zweig, added in two thousand three.
Zweig follows each of Graham's chapters with a modern chapter of his own, and it is genuinely valuable, because he is able to take Graham's abstract warnings and lay the recent wreckage beside them.
When Graham warns about new issues, Zweig can show you the dot-com IPOs of nineteen ninety nine, doubling on the first day and then falling ninety five percent.
When Graham warns about reported earnings, Zweig can walk you through Enron and WorldCom.
When Graham describes Mr. Market's manic phase, Zweig can quote the analysts of the year two thousand.
The commentary makes the case that Graham was not describing his era.
He was describing a permanent feature of crowds.
The second is Graham's own late change of mind, which the honest telling requires.
In an interview in nineteen seventy six, the last year of his life, Graham said he no longer advocated elaborate techniques of security analysis to find superior value opportunities.
That had been a rewarding activity forty years earlier, he said, when his textbook was first published, but the situation had changed.

Enormous research effort was now being poured into the market by very many people, and he doubted that in most cases such extensive effort would generate sufficiently superior selections to justify the cost.

He was, at the end, in favor of a simplified, rules-based approach, applied to a broad group of stocks, which for most people today means something very close to a low cost index fund plus a rebalancing policy.
There is a coda to all of this that is worth knowing, because it is the best answer ever given to the objection that Graham's approach is just luck dressed up.
In nineteen eighty four, on the fiftieth anniversary of the textbook Graham wrote with David Dodd, Buffett gave a talk at Columbia called The Superinvestors of Graham-and-Doddsville.
The academic fashion of the day held that markets were efficient, that nobody could beat them consistently, and that anyone who appeared to had simply been lucky.
Buffett's response was a thought experiment.
Imagine, he said, that all two hundred and twenty five million Americans enter a national coin-flipping contest.
Everyone bets a dollar and flips.
Losers drop out.
After twenty mornings of this, about two hundred and fifteen people would remain, each having called twenty flips in a row, each now worth a bit over a million dollars.
And these people would, he said, get insufferable.
They would write books called How I Turned a Dollar into a Million in Twenty Days While Working Thirty Seconds a Morning.
And the professors would rightly point out that if you started with two hundred and twenty five million orangutans instead, you would get exactly the same result.
Twenty flips is twenty flips.
But then, Buffett said, suppose you discovered that forty of those two hundred and fifteen winning orangutans came from the same zoo.
You would go and ask the zookeeper what he was feeding them.
A concentration that extreme demands an explanation.
And that, he argued, is what you find with Graham's students.
He went through them one by one, with the actual audited records.
Walter Schloss, who had no college education, worked out of a small office with no research staff, and simply bought statistically cheap stocks for decades.
Tom Knapp.
Bill Ruane of the Sequoia Fund.
Charlie Munger.
Rick Guerin.
Stan Perlmeter, who had been in advertising.

These people had wildly different personalities, different temperaments, different portfolios, they rarely owned the same stocks, and several of them Buffett had recruited or met through Graham's orbit.
What they shared was one intellectual origin: they all sought the gap between price and value, and they all demanded a margin of safety before acting.
And they all, over long periods, beat the market by margins that luck does not comfortably explain.
Buffett's point was that the framework travels.
It is not a personality trait and it is not a gift.
It is a way of thinking that can be handed from one person to another, which is precisely what a book is for.
I find Graham's late admission moving rather than deflating.
The man spent his life building an analytical apparatus, and when the evidence changed he said so, in public, in his eighties.
It is the margin of safety principle applied to his own opinions.
And it points at something important about what this book is actually for.
If you take Graham as a stock picking manual, much of it is dated, and he told you so himself.
If you take it as a book about temperament, almost none of it has aged at all.
Because the argument underneath everything is this.
Investing success does not depend on being cleverer than other people.

Graham says explicitly that it takes no great intelligence to be a successful investor, and Buffett has said that once you are past an ordinary IQ, what you need is not more brain but more control of the urges that get others into trouble.
What it depends on is a sound framework, held consistently, that protects you from your own reactions.
The intelligent investor in Graham's title, he tells us, is not the one who forecasts well or trades cleverly.
It is a matter of character much more than of brainpower.

It is the person who is realistic enough to demand a margin of safety, patient enough to accept an adequate return, businesslike enough to look at the accounts, and disciplined enough to treat Mr. Market as a servant rather than a guide.
So let me gather the whole thing into a single shape before I leave you with the practical part.

A man who watched his mother ruined by a margin account and who was then ruined himself in nineteen twenty nine set out to write down how a person could put money at work without being at the mercy of the crowd.
He began by separating investment from speculation, insisting that anything without thorough analysis, safety of principal and an adequate return be called by its true name.

He divided investors not into brave and timid but into those who will do the work and those who will not, and told the second group to adopt a simple policy of stocks and bonds with fixed limits and mechanical rebalancing, because a rule you can keep beats a strategy you abandon in March.

He gave us Mr. Market, the manic depressive partner who shows up with a price every day, whose quotations exist for our convenience and never for our instruction, and who will not be offended if we ignore him for a decade.

He gave us the margin of safety, the engineering discipline of buying so far below your estimate of value that being wrong is survivable, whose true function is to make an accurate forecast of the future unnecessary.

He told us that investment is most intelligent when it is most businesslike, that we own pieces of enterprises rather than symbols, and that we are neither right nor wrong because the crowd disagrees with us, only because our facts and reasoning are right or wrong.
And he warned us, repeatedly, patiently, that the enemy in this is not the market.
It is the person holding the account.
So let me leave you with the practical heart of it, the things you can do starting this week.
Write down, honestly, whether you are the defensive investor or the enterprising one, and be brutal about it.
Not which you would like to be, but how many hours a month you will actually spend reading financial statements.
If the honest answer is close to zero, that is not a failing.
Graham thought that person could do perfectly well.
What Graham thought would fail is the person who does two hours and behaves as though they had done two hundred.
Set your stock and bond allocation in advance, in writing, with an upper and lower bound you will not cross, and set a rebalancing rule with it.
Whether it is Graham's twenty five to seventy five or something else, the value comes from deciding it now, while nothing is on fire, and then executing it mechanically when something is.
Before you buy anything, write down what the business is worth and why, in a few sentences, and then compare that to the price.
If you cannot write the paragraph, you are not investing in Graham's sense, and you should either do the work or buy the index.
Insist on a real gap between your estimate of value and the price you pay.
Not a five percent gap.
A gap wide enough that you could be substantially wrong about the business and still not lose money.
Stop treating price movements as information about a business.
When a holding falls thirty percent, the only relevant question is whether the underlying enterprise changed.
If it did not, Mr. Market has just made you an offer, not delivered a verdict.
Never buy something because it has been rising, and never buy a new issue in a hot market, for the simple structural reason that the seller chose the timing and the seller knows more than you do.
And judge any single year's earnings against a seven to ten year average, because one year tells you almost nothing about a business and quite a lot about the accountants.
